documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Aiuta

documents.t: Aiuta's core business is shopper-facing virtual try-on for enterprise retail. Shoppers upload a photo and see themselves in an item in seconds, building single looks or complete outfits. It deploys via SDK or API and is designed to slot into existing ecommerce infrastructure with minimal engineering lift. The customer list is the strongest part of the story: ASOS, About You, Alice + Olivia, adidas Originals, Namshi, HEMCO, Tanya Taylor, and Leset. Aiuta Studio is the second product and works differently from most tools in this comparison. A brand supplies basic product images; the platform returns studio-grade outputs with custom backgrounds and lighting, including flat-lay conversion from model shots. Two details define the experience: every output passes human QA before delivery, with a stated 95% first-pass acceptance rate, and turnaround is quoted at 24–48 hours. That QA guarantee is a real differentiator against pure self-serve generators, and it is also the shape of a service. You submit, you wait, you receive. Neither Aiuta page we reviewed publishes pricing for Studio.
documents.s: Aiuta: try-on infrastructure, with a studio attached

documents.t: Astria puts the creative decision inside the brand. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored, editable, and reusable by the people who own the brand's look. The immediate consequence is iteration speed. A creative director who wants a warmer background, a tighter crop, or different casting changes the treatment and re-runs; there is no submission and no return cycle. The second consequence is coverage: templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial alongside apparel, and the same direction extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Aiuta's evidence is enterprise retail try-on, and it is genuinely impressive at that: recognizable global retailers running its shopper experience. We found no named customer references specifically for Aiuta Studio in the material reviewed, and no published performance metrics on the shopper-experience page beyond capability claims. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published in both cases. The relevant question is which body of evidence matches the job you are buying for.
documents.s: Public proof: retail deployment versus production adoption

documents.t: Consider a retailer already running Aiuta try-on across its apparel catalog. The ecommerce director likes the vendor, the integration is stable, and Studio promises catalog imagery from the same contract. Consolidating suppliers is a legitimately good instinct. Here is how the season plays out. Product images go in; polished outputs come back within 24–48 hours, QA-checked, and the acceptance rate is high. Then the creative director sees the first batch and wants the crop 15% wider and the light cooler. That is a new submission and another cycle. Two weeks later a campaign brief lands that needs editorial framing rather than catalog framing, and that is outside what the studio product is aimed at. The lookbook needs a different answer again. The consolidation saved a vendor relationship and did not save the production. With Astria, the crop change is an edit to the approved treatment, applied instantly across everything already produced and everything still to come. The campaign frames and lookbook come from the same treatment rather than a different supplier. And the try-on integration—if the retailer wants it—stays exactly where it is, doing the job it is genuinely good at.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: the consolidation temptation

documents.t: This is Aiuta's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Rendering a specific shopper into a garment in seconds, deployed at ASOS and adidas Originals scale, with SDK and API integration paths, is hard infrastructure that Astria does not build. Retailers whose bottleneck is fit confidence at the point of purchase should evaluate Aiuta on those merits and not expect a production tool to substitute.
documents.s: Enterprise shopper-facing try-on — winner: Aiuta

documents.t: A QA-checked delivery pipeline is dependable precisely because it is standardized, and standardization is the opposite of art direction. In Astria the treatment is the brand's object: editable by the brand's creative director, visible to the brand's team, and applied on the brand's schedule.
documents.s: Who holds the creative decision — winner: Astria

documents.t: A 24–48 hour turnaround is excellent for a service and slow for a decision. Creative work converges through rapid, cheap iteration; a delivery cycle makes each iteration a scheduled event. This is the single biggest practical difference between buying finished images and running production.
documents.s: Iteration speed — winner: Astria

documents.t: Aiuta Studio is aimed at product photography. A season also needs lookbook, campaign, editorial, social, and motion, all sharing one visual language. Astria produces those from a single approved direction, which is both fewer suppliers and a more coherent result.
documents.s: Coverage of the season — winner: Astria

documents.t: Aiuta advertises diverse AI models intended to reflect a brand's customers, which is the right ambition. Astria's reusable library goes further into production requirements: ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that persist across seasons.
documents.s: Casting depth — winner: Astria

documents.t: Aiuta's team surface is technical integration. Astria's is creative review: private brand workspaces, a multiplayer Board with named cursors, and live voice over the actual canvas, with the photographer, in-house studio, and agency all inside the same workspace.
documents.s: Collaboration and review — winner: Astria

documents.t: Studio throughput is bounded by the QA and delivery cycle, and no pricing is published, so a brand cannot model a season before entering a sales process. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work—import the SKU set from Shopify or Google Drive, run it against the approved setup—with brand pricing scoped to usage: pay for what you create. No claim is made here that Astria is cheaper. The point is that a delivery cycle you cannot price is hard to plan a season around; model a full collection, including revisions, before comparing.
documents.s: Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria

documents.t: After a year with a delivery service, a brand has a large set of finished files. After a year with Astria, it has the files plus the casting, references, templates, and approvals that produced them—and the next season starts from those.
documents.s: Compounding production value — winner: Astria

documents.t: Shopper-facing virtual try-on at enterprise retail scale is the primary purchase. You want catalog imagery delivered as a QA-checked service rather than produced in-house. A 24–48 hour turnaround fits your production calendar. SDK or API integration into an existing ecommerce stack is a requirement.
documents.s: Choose Aiuta if...

documents.t: Your creative director should be able to change direction without a delivery cycle. One approved creative direction must carry across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion. Casting depth across ages and body types is a production requirement. Your photographer, studio, and agency need to work in the same workspace. You want the creative recipe at the end of the season, not only the files.
documents.s: Choose Astria if...

documents.t: For fashion brands producing their own imagery, Astria is the stronger choice: the creative decision stays with the people who own it, and iteration costs minutes rather than days. Aiuta is a serious enterprise try-on vendor, and its studio service is a reasonable convenience for retailers who want finished catalog files—just not a substitute for owning production. Consolidating vendors is sound procurement. Consolidating your art direction into a delivery queue is not.
documents.s: The bottom line

documents.t: Run five representative SKUs through both, then deliberately change the creative direction after the first batch is approved. Measure elapsed time for that change in each path — that number is the comparison. Ask Aiuta for Studio-specific customer references and published pricing. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, check what happens when a campaign or lookbook brief arrives mid-season.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Ayna

documents.t: Ayna positions itself as an AI photoshoot platform for fashion ecommerce brands. Upload a flat-lay, mannequin, or existing on-model photo, pick a model from an attribute-built library, choose a background, pose, and accessories, and Ayna generates the on-model shot—then rounds out the listing with a short product video, AI-written titles and descriptions, and a direct push to Shopify. Marketplace tooling is a real strength: compliant crops, ghost mannequins, platform-specific ratios, and bulk runs across large SKU batches. Ayna's own materials are candid about the job it does: it replaces the studio, the videographer, and the copywriter for routine catalog and marketplace work. That is a precise description of both the value and the boundary. The model library is deep—Ayna advertises over 1,000 attribute-built AI models, with brand-locked custom models on higher plans—and the categories skew toward marketplace-driven segments such as kidswear, ethnic wear, and plus-size.
documents.s: Ayna: listing automation from a single flat-lay

documents.t: Astria approaches the same category from the brand's side rather than the marketplace's. It gives fashion teams a workspace where products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together, so an approved look becomes a reusable recipe rather than a one-off generation. Templates cover fashion-specific categories beyond standard apparel PDPs—beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial—and brand references keep results anchored to the brand rather than a generic AI aesthetic. Teams operate the approved workflow without becoming prompt experts, and creative decisions survive personnel changes because they are encoded in the workspace.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Ayna's case-study library is genuine adoption evidence, concentrated in marketplace-first fashion: customer stories describe Zucchini scaling catalog throughput on Myntra, Aditya Birla Fashion cutting per-SKU photoshoot spend, and D2C labels launching without a physical shoot. Ayna also reports 3,000+ brands and over a million images generated as self-reported platform data. These are vendor-written accounts rather than independent benchmarks, but they show real listing-volume adoption, including at enterprise brand houses. Astria's public materials show a professional production base: recognizable brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work on the platform. This is also vendor-published evidence, but the signal points toward brand-directed production—lookbooks, campaigns, and social—rather than listing automation alone.
documents.s: Public proof: marketplace throughput versus professional production

documents.t: Imagine a brand launching 60 garments needing four PDP images per SKU, a small lookbook, paid-social variations, and a late colorway addition. With Ayna, the team uploads flat-lays, picks models and scene presets, and generates listings quickly—including marketplace variations and AI-written copy pushed straight to the store. The arithmetic deserves attention, though: 60 SKUs at four shots each is 240 images, which is the entire yearly image allowance of Ayna's entry plan before a single regeneration, and regenerations are capped per image. Each listing is also an independent generation: the lookbook, the social variants, and the late colorway each start from menu choices again, and image corrections route through an edit queue measured in working days. With Astria, the team defines casting, styling, lighting, and format once, approves the treatment, and runs the collection against it. The late colorway inherits the approved setup automatically. Campaign crops and video extend the same direction instead of restarting it, and reviewers work on the same board rather than trading screenshots.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: a seasonal drop

documents.t: Ayna's menus—models, scenes, poses, accessories—make each listing fast, and custom templates on higher plans add some reuse. But the unit of work remains the individual listing, and a menu of presets is not the same as encoding a brand's casting, styling, and art direction. Astria makes the approved direction itself the reusable asset: it persists across SKUs, channels, and contributors, and compounds over a season.
documents.s: Creative direction and repeatability — winner: Astria

documents.t: Ayna advertises fashion-grade realism and photoreal models, and its marketplace acceptance evidence suggests the routine case works. Its correction workflow, however, is metered: plans include one to three regenerations per image, and photoshoot edits carry a one-to-three-working-day turnaround depending on tier. Astria treats refinement as part of the workflow: a dedicated face-inpainting and refinement pass improves facial detail, skin, hair, and texture inside the production loop, without consuming a capped correction budget or waiting on a queue.
documents.s: Natural-looking people and corrections — winner: Astria

documents.t: Ayna's video product generates 10-second catalog and reel clips, metered per second of generation and capped per plan. That covers PDP motion. Astria offers a choice of current video-generation options so an approved still can be animated without leaving the workspace, alongside campaign, editorial, and social formats drawn from the same source assets.
documents.s: Stills, motion, and formats — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is Ayna's genuine edge, and the one concession that matters: no other tool in this comparison turns a flat-lay into a complete, publishable listing—image, video, title, description, marketplace-compliant crops—and pushes it to Shopify in one flow, from a self-serve plan a team can start on today. It is a listing-operations advantage, not a creative-production verdict: the same pipeline that automates the routine listing standardizes it, and the brand's creative direction lives outside the tool.
documents.s: Listing automation and marketplace publishing — winner: Ayna

documents.t: Ayna's bulk runs produce marketplace variations at volume, but the commercial model meters the work: yearly image allowances, per-image credits, capped regenerations, and seat limits by plan. At collection scale the bill and the caps track every SKU, colorway, channel, and retry. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work—the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive, the approved setup runs across it—and brand pricing is scoped to usage: pay for what you create, sized to the production engagement. A per-image allowance is not a production budget; model a full collection, including rework, before comparing costs.
documents.s: Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria

documents.t: Ayna offers team seats—one on the entry plan, up to ten on the highest published tier. Astria combines private brand workspaces with a multiplayer Board: teammates see named cursors, talk over the actual canvas with live voice, and resolve looks together. And the work accumulates: products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs carry from the collection into campaigns, video, and social, so the photographer, in-house studio, and social agency share one source of truth instead of a folder of exported listings.
documents.s: Collaborative production and compounding value — winner: Astria

A self-serve start with published per-seat plans matters more than owning the creative direction. Your inputs are flat-lays or mannequin shots and the standard on-model treatment is acceptable. Listing enrichment and direct Shopify publishing are the core of the job.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Browzwear

documents.t: Browzwear's platform is built around a serious idea: if a virtual garment behaves like the physical one, most of product development can happen before anything is cut. VStitcher creates what the company calls accurate virtual twins of physical garments, combining AI-driven fit intelligence with true-to-life 3D simulation. Designers work across 2D drafting and 3D draping, fit on customizable avatars, grade across sizes, use tension and pressure mapping, and export tech packs with detailed specifications. Fabric Analyzer measures real fabric properties so the simulation is grounded in the actual material. Stylezone handles collection collaboration; the Open Platform handles integrations. The claimed outcomes are the ones a product development director cares about: 50–80% fewer physical samples, 95% first-time-right samples, double the development speed, 35% total cost reduction. The company cites over 1,000 apparel companies and 10 million digital garments created, with brands including Nike, Puma, Under Armour, Target, Walmart, and VF Corporation. These are vendor-published figures rather than independent benchmarks, but the adoption base in this space is not in question. Browzwear also states that the platform generates technical and ecommerce assets. That is true, and it is the sentence that brings buyers to this comparison.
documents.s: Browzwear: getting the garment right before it exists

documents.t: Astria starts where Browzwear's job ends. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—becomes the reusable unit that produces the season's imagery. The inputs are the difference. Astria works from the product photography a brand already has, not from a digital twin built to manufacturing tolerances. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial alongside apparel, and the same approved direction extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion. The people operating it are the brand's creative and ecommerce team, or the photographer or agency they work with—not a 3D department.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Browzwear's proof is deep and industrial: a thousand-plus apparel companies, household-name brands, and three decades of digital product creation. Read it for what it demonstrates—that 3D design and development works at scale in real supply chains. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them, including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published. Neither set of evidence transfers to the other's domain, which is the honest summary of this whole comparison.
documents.s: Public proof: development adoption versus production adoption

documents.t: Consider a sportswear brand that adopted 3D development two years ago. Roughly half its styles have digital twins. The ecommerce team asks the obvious question: can we skip the photoshoot? Rendering from Browzwear is possible, and for the styles that have production-ready twins it can look excellent, because the garment geometry and fabric behavior are real rather than inferred. But the path has costs that do not appear on a license: only half the line qualifies, so the other half needs a different solution anyway; each render needs a 3D artist to build the scene, light it, and produce the frames; the avatars are fit avatars rather than cast models with a brand's point of view; and a request for a warmer campaign crop is a rendering job, not an edit. Producing 400 SKUs across four channels this way is a studio operation staffed with specialists. With Astria, the same team works from the product photography it already produces. Casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format get approved once, the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive, and the collection runs against that treatment. The styles with digital twins and the ones without are handled identically. Campaign and social extend the same direction, and motion animates stills that already passed review. The two are not in conflict. The 3D investment keeps paying for itself upstream—fewer samples, better fit, faster development—while imagery production stops depending on which styles happen to have twins.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: the brand with 3D already in the building

documents.t: This is Browzwear's genuine edge and the one concession that matters, and it is a large one. True-to-life fabric physics, tension and pressure mapping, size grading, and tech pack generation solve problems that no image-generation product addresses, including Astria. If your objective is fewer physical samples, better first-fit rates, or a shorter development calendar, Browzwear is the answer and this comparison should not talk you out of it.

Producing imagery in Astria requires a product photo and an approved template. For a design team with twins for every style and 3D artists on staff, the first path is viable. For everyone else, the prerequisite is the obstacle.

documents.t: Caimera positions itself as an AI photo studio for ecommerce brands. Its Fluid tool transforms a single product shot into editorial-style imagery, while its Click tool swaps models and backgrounds on existing on-model or mannequin photos. A bulk catalog flow converts flat lays to on-model shots at volume, and the company advertises upscale quality suitable for billboard use. The workflow is deliberately prompt-light: upload a product, pick a template or describe a scene, generate, and refine with editing tools. A campaign ideas tool can read a brand's website or Pinterest board and propose moodboards. Caimera's own help documentation notes that Fluid works best when garment accuracy is not the top priority and recommends Click for delicate fabrics, textures, and sheer materials—an honest boundary that matters for demanding fashion work.
documents.s: Caimera: fast self-serve fashion imagery

documents.t: Astria approaches the same category from the opposite direction. Instead of optimizing a single transformation, it gives fashion teams a workspace where products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together. An approved look becomes a reusable recipe rather than a one-off generation. Templates cover fashion-specific categories beyond standard apparel PDPs, and brand references keep results anchored to the brand rather than a generic AI aesthetic. Teams can operate the approved workflow without becoming prompt experts, and creative decisions survive personnel changes because they are encoded in the workspace, not in someone's chat history.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Caimera's case-study library is genuinely useful evidence: Adore Me, BlissClub, Floafers, Ioni Swim, and Maggie the Label describe measurable outcomes—higher click-through rates, lower CPAs, and large production-cost reductions. These are vendor-written accounts rather than independent benchmarks, but they show real commercial adoption, particularly for advertising imagery. Astria's public materials show a broader professional base: recognizable brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work on the platform. This is also vendor-published evidence, but the signal points toward professional production use rather than purely self-serve image generation.

documents.t: Imagine a brand launching 60 garments needing four PDP images per SKU, a small lookbook, paid-social variations, and a late colorway addition. With Caimera, the team uploads products, runs the bulk catalog flow, uses templates and the campaign ideas tool for social variants, and generates VooDoo videos for ads. Credit consumption is predictable and the queue moves fast. Each image, however, is largely an independent generation: changing the colorway or extending the campaign means re-entering prompts and re-checking consistency manually. With Astria, the team defines casting, styling, lighting, and format once, approves the treatment, and runs the collection against it. The late colorway inherits the approved setup automatically. Campaign crops and video extend the same direction instead of restarting it, and reviewers work on the same board rather than trading screenshots.

documents.t: Caimera's templates and moodboard tool accelerate ideation, but the unit of work remains the individual image. Astria makes the approved direction itself the reusable asset: casting, styling, scene, crop, and format persist across SKUs, channels, and contributors. That distinction compounds over a season.

documents.t: Both platforms take garment accuracy seriously, and Caimera's Click tool preserves garments well when starting from fitted product photography. But Caimera's documentation concedes Fluid's limits on intricate and sheer garments, and realism depends on which tool fits the input. Astria adds a dedicated face-inpainting and refinement pass that improves facial detail, skin, hair, and texture inside the workflow—a finishing layer rather than a manual correction request.

documents.t: Caimera's VooDoo agent produces short fashion videos, which covers many ad needs. documents.t: Caimera supports team collaboration from its Starter plan and human Photoshop requests on higher tiers. Astria combines private brand workspaces with a multiplayer Board: teammates see named cursors, talk over the actual canvas, and resolve looks together—closer to a studio review than a ticketing queue.

documents.t: This is Caimera's genuine edge, and the one concession that matters: a free tier and published plans from $15 per user per month mean a team can start the same day, without a sales conversation. It is an onboarding advantage, not a production-cost verdict—those plans meter per-image credits, so at collection scale the bill tracks how many generations, and regenerations, the work actually takes.

Astria treats the collection as the unit of work: the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive, the approved setup runs across it, and brand pricing is scoped to usage and the production engagement rather than metered image by image. A per-image price is not a production budget—model a full collection, including rework, before comparing costs.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs DRESSX

documents.t: DRESSX has been in digital fashion since 2020 and has converged on a clear enterprise proposition: an AI suite for fashion and luxury brands, sold as modules. Virtual try-on is the flagship, answering the question the company puts at the center of its pitch—whether an item will actually look good on the shopper. It handles single items, full looks, and mix-and-match, integrates through an API, a white-label option, or a Shopify plugin, and the company advertises very fast integration. Around it sit adjacent products: an AI customer assistant, an AI stylist for retail, and DRESSX Mirror, a human-sized interactive screen for stores, pop-ups, window displays, and events. Named implementations include Victoria Beckham and Farfetch. The published outcome claims are aimed squarely at ecommerce leadership: a 40% reduction in return rate, a 3.2× conversion lift, 68% higher engagement, and up to 75% fit certainty. These are vendor-published figures without disclosed methodology, and a buyer should ask how they were measured and over what baseline. But they are the right metrics for what DRESSX sells, and they are not metrics a content production tool should be claiming.

documents.t: Astria's job starts earlier in the funnel and further back in the calendar. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—becomes the reusable unit that produces the season. That covers the assets a try-on experience cannot: the PDP images a shopper sees before deciding to engage, the lookbook that frames the collection, the campaign that drives traffic, the social cutdowns, and the motion. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial alongside apparel, and the same approved direction runs across the whole SKU set imported from Shopify or Google Drive.

documents.t: DRESSX publishes brand implementations and conversion-oriented statistics. Read them as evidence that the experience layer gets deployed by serious retailers, and probe the methodology in a demo. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published. Neither company's evidence speaks to the other's domain, which is the accurate summary of this comparison.

documents.t: Trace a single customer journey for a spring dress. She sees a paid-social video, clicks through to a campaign landing page, browses the collection grid, opens the product page, scrolls the four PDP images and a detail shot, then taps "try it on." DRESSX owns the last step of that journey and does it well. Everything before it—the social video, the campaign frame, the collection grid, the five PDP images—is content the brand had to produce. If the answer to producing it was a photoshoot, DRESSX has not changed the brand's production economics at all; it has improved the conversion rate on assets that still cost what they always cost. With Astria, that entire upstream chain comes from one approved treatment: the campaign frame, the grid, the PDP set, the detail crop, and the social video all derive from the same casting, styling, and direction, run across the collection. The try-on button at the end is a complementary purchase, not an alternative one.

Brands whose live problem is return rates or fit hesitation should evaluate DRESSX on that basis, ask hard questions about how the published lift figures were measured, and not expect a content production tool to substitute.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Emilia AI Studio

documents.t: Emilia's promise is compact and well executed: upload a product photo, pick a style, get campaign-ready images in seconds. Three output types anchor the experience—clean packshot, with presenter, and lifestyle scene—and six category libraries supply the style presets. Campaign kits produce ready-made sets of four images, applied all at once or chosen individually. The editor is the part that stands out. Users draw on an image to mark a region, then describe the change or drop a reference image; there are move and remove operations, a proper filter set spanning instant film, teal and orange, high-key and low-key, bleach bypass, rim light, noir and more, plus background removal, simple and advanced expand, aspect-ratio resizing across eight ratios, and AI super-resolution up to 4K. That is more genuine editing craft than most self-serve generators in this category offer. Practical touches are sensible too: a WooCommerce plugin and CSV upload for catalog import, bulk upload, a true free tier, and an interface available in English, Hebrew, and Spanish. The company describes itself as built by a digital agency, and it reports 150,000+ images generated, 5,000+ active businesses, 42+ countries, and around forty seconds per image. Two things a fashion buyer should read carefully. The first is what "Lookbook" means here: up to three variations of one product from different angles or focal points. Useful, and not what a fashion team means by a lookbook. The second is the plan structure, discussed below.
documents.s: Emilia AI Studio: breadth across the shelf

documents.t: Astria narrows to fashion and spends the depth there. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that produces a season. That means casting is a library rather than an entitlement, references accumulate rather than expiring against a storage cap, and templates encode the conventions of apparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work as production disciplines. Campaign frames, editorial spreads, social crops, and motion all derive from the same approved direction, and review happens on a multiplayer Board with named cursors and live voice, with external photographers and agencies inside the same workspace.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Emilia publishes volume statistics—images generated, active businesses, countries, average generation time. Those describe reach, and in the material we reviewed we found no named customer, case study, or testimonial. That is common for a self-serve product at this stage; it also means a buyer has nothing specific to verify. Astria's public materials name fashion brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published too, and at least checkable by looking.

documents.t: Consider a womenswear label with 60 styles going live, needing four images per style at 4K, plus campaign assets and social crops. It signs up on Emilia's Creator plan at $55 a month. The first week goes well. The editor is pleasant, packshots and lifestyle scenes look good, and the WooCommerce import saves real time. Then three constraints arrive together. Casting: the brand wants three recurring models for different segments of the line, and Creator allows five custom presenters, which is workable—but Starter would have allowed two, and a brand that grows into more distinct casting needs runs into a ceiling that is a billing conversation rather than a creative one. Credits: 60 styles at four 4K images each is 240 images at six credits, or roughly 1,440 credits, above Creator's 1,000 before a single rejected frame. Storage: the plan caps stored images, so a season's output has to be managed against a ceiling. Then the campaign brief lands. Campaign kits give four ready-made images per category, which is a starting point rather than a brand's campaign. A real lookbook is not three angle variations. Motion for social is not something we could verify the product does at all. With Astria, casting is a library the brand builds and keeps, the 60 styles run against one approved treatment, the campaign and editorial frames come from that same direction, and motion animates stills that already passed review. Nothing in the season is rationed by a plan tier.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: the day you need a third model

documents.t: This is Emilia's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Region-select editing with a reference-image drop, a real filter set, expand, background removal, and super-resolution gives an operator direct manual control over a finished frame, and several larger competitors in this category offer less. If your work is a modest number of images that each need individual attention, that toolkit is a real advantage.

documents.t: A product serving food, furniture, and apparel optimizes for what they share: a clean subject, a pleasing background, a consistent light. Fashion's hard parts are not shared—drape on a knit, how a sleeve breaks, casting that matches a brand's customer, a crop convention held across a collection. Emilia's jewelry and beauty categories are style presets for those product types; Astria's are production disciplines with their own casting, lighting, and framing logic.

documents.t: This is the sharpest structural difference. Emilia rations custom presenters by plan—one, two, five, eight, or twelve. For a seller shooting one product line that is generous. For a fashion brand, casting is not a feature allowance: a womenswear line, a kids range, and an extended-size offer are three casting requirements before anyone discusses campaigns. Astria treats casting as a reusable library, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that accumulate season over season.

documents.t: Style presets and campaign kits are chosen per generation; custom styles are capped and stored images have a ceiling. Astria stores the approved treatment itself, so the tenth SKU is produced the same way as the first by someone who was not there for the decision.

documents.t: Three angle variations are not a lookbook, and a four-image campaign kit is not a campaign. Editorial framing, social-native crops, and motion are separate disciplines, and Astria produces them as expressions of one approved direction rather than as presets applied to a product shot.
documents.s: Coverage of the season — winner: Astria

Astria's brand workspaces and multiplayer Board—named cursors, live voice over the production canvas—exist because fashion work passes between a stylist, an ecommerce lead, a photographer, and often an agency.

documents.t: FashionLab positions itself for brand and marketing teams producing on-brand AI content, and its core flow is a clean five-step batch: select garment references as flat lay or on-body, assign models, choose pose, choose background, then generate dozens of looks with consistent models and backgrounds. Generation times are quoted around ninety seconds, and the company is unusually candid about disclosing the underlying generation model it uses. Its casting options are broader than most small competitors: a free library of diverse AI models, custom brand-specific models, and the option to hire authorized digital twins of real models and influencers. Its published use cases include kids fashion—explicitly framed around avoiding the complexity of photoshoots with minors—and size inclusivity, both of which are real production needs that many tools in this category ignore. Credit where it is due: that is a thoughtful use-case set. The genuinely novel part is the Creative Marketplace. Brands can hire specialized talent for creative direction, prompting, retouching, and project management; creators can find paid projects from brands. A separate in-built professional retouching service handles polished finishing at scale. No other product in this comparison bundles a labour market with the software. The commercial structure needs care. The Basic plan is $20 a month and covers one brand and one project with two collaborator seats; extra seats are $20 a month each, four additional projects are $30 a month, and tokens are purchased separately at roughly $1.10–$1.20 each, with each generation consuming tokens according to resolution and complexity. Published proof is early: one named testimonial from a brand and marketing manager at Bruun Steengade, plus a reference to top Scandinavian brands.

documents.t: Astria's answer to the same problem is to make outside expertise less necessary each season. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored so the next person runs it rather than rebuilding it. That extends across categories and channels. Templates cover beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct disciplines; the casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references; and campaign, editorial, social, and motion all derive from the same direction. When a brand does bring in an outside photographer or art director, that person works inside the workspace and leaves the treatment behind.

Three lines against a plan built around one brand and one project means paid add-ons; a fourth collaborator means another $20 a month; and 200 SKUs at four images is 800 generations, which at roughly $1.10–$1.20 a token is a meaningful token bill before any rejected frame. documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs FASHN

documents.t: FASHN describes itself around a single clear promise: realistic images of your clothes, worn by anyone. It ships that promise in two forms. The app gives brands, agencies, and creators a set of tools—product to model, model swap, AI model creation, background removal, editing, reframing, 4K upscaling, face swap, and short video. The endpoint suite offers the same capabilities to other software: try-on at up to 4K, product to model, model swap, image to video, and more, with published latency ranges and language SDKs. The customer signal is worth reading closely. On the app side, FASHN publishes testimonials from fashion-adjacent businesses and marketplaces. On the endpoint side, the logos are largely other AI products and tools rather than fashion brands. That is not a criticism—it is an accurate picture of what FASHN sells best. It is a capability that other people build products and workflows around, and it is good enough at that job to have become infrastructure for a chunk of this category. FASHN also does real work on consistency. A face reference can anchor a specific look across generations, and model creation exposes control over age, body type, expression, and styling. A brand that needs the same face on 200 PDPs has a supported path.
documents.s: FASHN: a capability, packaged two ways

documents.t: Astria's unit of work is not the image; it is the treatment. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together in a brand workspace, so an approved look becomes something a team runs rather than something one operator recreates. The practical consequence is what carries forward. A face reference keeps a face consistent; an Astria template keeps the casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, and format consistent, then applies that whole treatment to the next SKU, the next colorway, and the next channel. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work, and Astria's Describe tool can turn a rights-cleared reference into usable creative direction while accounting for products and models already loaded.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: FASHN's published proof points to genuine traction in its own lane: named app testimonials from fashion businesses and a roster of software products building on its endpoints, alongside open-source model releases that earned it technical credibility. These are vendor-published signals rather than independent benchmarks. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them: recognizable names including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, plus studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published, and also an adoption signal rather than a quality proof—but it points at a different buyer. FASHN's strongest evidence is that developers ship with it. Astria's is that fashion teams produce with it.

documents.t: Consider a small creative agency producing seasonal content for three fashion clients: catalog imagery for one, a lookbook and campaign for another, social-first content for the third. Different casting, different visual language, different approvers. With FASHN, the agency works tool by tool. Product to model for the catalog shots, model swap where a client supplies existing on-model photography, a face reference per client to hold casting steady, then editing and reframing for channel variants. It works, and for individual assets it works quickly. But each client's visual language lives in the operator's head and in a set of remembered settings; seats are capped by plan; and automating the catalog client's volume means building against the endpoints, which is an engineering project, not a production feature. With Astria, each client gets a private brand workspace. The agency defines the treatment once per client, approves it, and runs the collection against it. Client approvers join the multiplayer Board and review the actual canvas with voice rather than receiving a folder of exports. When the catalog client adds a colorway in week six, it inherits the approved setup instead of restarting it—and when the agency hands the workflow back to the client's in-house team, the recipe goes with it.

documents.t: FASHN is organized around operations. You pick a tool, supply an input, get an output. That is the right shape for try-on, and it is a poor shape for a season, because nothing above the individual image is durable. Astria is organized around the treatment: the approved combination of casting, styling, scene, crop, and format that a brand wants repeated. Once that exists, running the next SKU is an execution step rather than a fresh creative decision.

documents.t: This is FASHN's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. If the requirement is try-on—shopper-facing, inside your own product, at 4K, with documented latency and language SDKs—FASHN is built for exactly that and Astria is not. Teams whose roadmap item is "add try-on to our app" should choose FASHN and stop reading. That is a real and well-executed job; it is simply a different job from producing a brand's campaign and catalog imagery.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Fermat

documents.t: Fermat calls itself the generative AI toolbox used by global fashion and luxury brands, and its reference list backs the claim: S.Oliver Group, ASOS, Tendam, PUIG, Desigual, Riachuelo, and Children's Apparel Network. That is a serious set of names, and notably they are fashion names—unlike several general creative platforms whose marquee logos come from other industries. The product is organized as tools rather than as a workflow. More than fifty of them cover sketch-to-render, parametric design modification, extracting graphics and prints from reference imagery, and visualizing garments on models. For ecommerce work specifically, Fermat describes pulling garments out of styled imagery to produce clean flat-lays, then visualizing on models, adjusting backgrounds and poses, and exporting up to 4K. It publishes efficiency claims of 75–80% reduction on core design tasks and 192× faster outfit visualization; both are vendor figures without disclosed methodology. The differentiator that closes deals is the wrapper. SOC2 Type II, SSO, on-premise deployment options, private models that do not train on customer data, and an explicit statement that generations belong to the customer. For a luxury group whose archive is the crown jewel, that combination is not a nice-to-have. Pricing is published, which is welcome: roughly $30 a month for 150 credits at the individual tier, $250 a month for 500 credits with unlimited users at the team tier, and custom enterprise. One credit per image, four per video.
documents.s: Fermat: a toolbox with a procurement-ready wrapper

documents.t: Astria is organized around producing a collection rather than around a toolkit. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit. The difference is what happens on the second SKU. A toolbox applies an operation again; a treatment applies a decision again. Astria's templates cover beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct categories; the casting library spans ages and body types including children and extended sizes; and campaign, editorial, social, and motion all derive from the same approved direction.

documents.t: Fermat's evidence sits with design departments at large fashion groups, which is exactly where its product is aimed and is genuinely strong. Read it as proof that the toolbox earns a place in a luxury design workflow. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published in both cases; the difference is which function inside a brand is doing the adopting.

documents.t: Consider a mid-size group where the design team already uses Fermat and the ecommerce team is choosing how to produce the season's imagery. The design team's experience is good, and the tools fit how designers work: extract a print from a reference, modify a silhouette, visualize the piece on a model before the sample exists. Credits are cheap per image, security cleared review, and the archive stays private. Extending that into production is where the shape strains. Producing 250 SKUs across PDP, detail, campaign, and social means running tools repeatedly rather than running an approved treatment; the brand's crop and casting conventions live in whoever operates the tools; casting for the children's line and macro conventions for jewelry are outside the library's depth; and when the freelance art director wants to review, the natural unit is exported files rather than a shared canvas. The 500-credit team tier covers 500 images a month, which a 250-SKU catalog at four images each exceeds in a single push. With Astria, the ecommerce team defines the treatment once with the art director inside the workspace, imports the SKU set from Shopify or Google Drive, and runs it. Campaign, social, and motion extend the same direction. The design team keeps Fermat, because nothing about this replaces sketch-to-render or print extraction.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Figma Weave

documents.t: Figma acquired Weavy on October 30, 2025 and relaunched it as Figma Weave. The product's premise, in Figma's own framing, is that the first prompt is a creative starting point rather than a final destination—so generation and hands-on craft belong in the same place. In practice that means a node-based canvas where outputs from many current models can be combined, branched, and refined, with professional editing operations—inpaint, outpaint, relight, upscale, crop, masking, color work—applied as part of the graph rather than in a separate tool. Model coverage is deliberately broad across image, video, and 3D. Workflows are reusable: a author builds the graph once, and Figma Weave can generate a simplified interface so teammates can run it without touching the nodes. Since 2026 a set of Weave tools and community workflows has been reachable directly inside Figma Design. It is genuinely excellent software. It is also, by intent, a general creative environment—the published examples span ad generation, product photography, illustration, storyboarding, and 3D rendering. Nothing in it is specifically about fashion.
documents.s: Figma Weave: a canvas for building creative pipelines

documents.t: Astria makes the opposite trade. Instead of a canvas that can express any workflow, it supplies a workflow that already understands fashion: products, casting, references, templates, and outputs in a brand workspace, with the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—as the reusable unit. The practical difference is what you start with. A fashion template for footwear, jewelry, beauty, or editorial work already encodes the conventions of that category. A casting library already spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting. The SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive rather than being wired up. Astria's Describe tool can extract usable direction from a rights-cleared reference while accounting for products and models already loaded. None of that is a node graph anyone had to author.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Figma Weave's evidence is its adoption across creative disciplines—independent creatives, startups, and enterprise teams including architects, VFX artists, marketers, and designers—and the credibility of the Figma platform around it. That is a strong signal for general creative production and says nothing specific about fashion catalogs. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published, and narrow on purpose.
documents.s: Public proof: creative breadth versus fashion production

documents.t: Consider a brand with 200 SKUs, a small creative team, and a design lead who is fluent in Figma. The Figma Weave path is attractive because the design lead can build exactly what the brand wants: a graph that takes a product photo, places it on a generated model, applies the brand's lighting treatment, produces four crops, and upscales. Once built, the team can run it behind a simplified interface. The costs are real but easy to overlook. Someone has to design that graph and keep it working; the fashion judgment inside it—how this brand casts, how a knit should fall, what crop convention the PDP uses—is knowledge the graph author supplies, not knowledge the tool contributes; and every new category, a jewelry capsule, say, is a new graph. When the design lead leaves, the pipeline becomes an artifact nobody fully understands. The Astria path starts further along. The team picks a fashion template appropriate to the category, loads the products, sets casting and styling, approves the treatment, and runs the SKU set imported from Shopify or Google Drive. What the brand maintains is a creative decision, not a piece of software. When someone new arrives, they inherit an approved treatment rather than a graph.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: who builds the pipeline

documents.t: This is the whole comparison. A node canvas is infinitely expressive and completely uninformed: it will happily build a beautiful pipeline that gets a garment's drape wrong, because nothing in it knows what drape is. Astria's templates, casting library, and product-reference handling exist because fashion has conventions worth encoding once. Flexibility is valuable when your outputs are unpredictable; supplied domain knowledge is valuable when they are not.
documents.s: Supplied knowledge versus built knowledge — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is Figma Weave's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Combining many current models with professional editing operations—relight, inpaint, matte work, compositing—inside a single node graph, reachable from the design environment a team already uses, is a real capability advantage for creative work in general. Teams whose output spans ads, illustration, motion design, and product imagery will get more from that breadth than from any fashion-specific system, and they should choose accordingly.

documents.t: Figma Weave's answer is thoughtful: workflow authors can publish a simplified UI so teammates run the graph without editing nodes. But that still divides the team into people who can change the workflow and people who cannot. In Astria, changing the crop convention or the casting is an edit to the treatment, made by the person who owns the creative decision.
documents.s: Who can run it without help — winner: Astria

documents.t: A season is catalog, detail, lookbook, campaign, editorial, social, and motion, produced consistently across a collection. Figma Weave can produce every one of those as an individual asset. Astria produces them as expressions of one approved direction, which is what makes them look like a collection rather than a set of executions.
documents.s: Coverage of a fashion season — winner: Astria

documents.t: Both scale, differently. Figma Weave scales a workflow once the workflow exists. Astria scales a creative decision: import the SKU set, run it against the approved treatment, extend into campaign and motion. The distinction matters most when the direction changes mid-season—an edit to a template versus a revision to a graph.
documents.s: Collection scale — winner: Astria

Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create, sized to the production. No claim is made here that Astria is cheaper; the point is that credits inside a design-seat subscription are a hard thing to map onto 200 SKUs across four channels. documents.t: FLORA describes itself as the AI-powered canvas for designers, brand teams, and agencies, and it has built a genuine fashion solution on top of that foundation. The pitch for fashion teams is end to end: from a sketch to a render, through colorways and fabrics, to on-model and campaign imagery, with batch application of one approved look across every SKU. It splits the experience into a Fashion Studio for everyday work and a Canvas for deeper ideation where models and steps chain together into reusable workflows. The platform breadth is real: FLORA advertises access to 50+ models spanning image, video, and multimodal reasoning under one subscription, with recognizable video models available for cinematic work. It has raised $42 million and its published references include Pentagram, Lionsgate, Base Design, and Hebbia. That reference list is the most useful signal for a fashion buyer. Pentagram is a design consultancy; Lionsgate is entertainment; Hebbia is enterprise software. They are impressive names and they attest to FLORA's quality as a creative environment. What the fashion solution page offers instead of brand case studies is credits to individual designers. For a brand evaluating who has actually run a season on the platform, that is a thinner evidence base than the platform's overall profile suggests.

documents.t: Astria is deliberately less ambitious in scope and more specific in depth. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that produces the season. Depth shows in the assets. The casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that accumulate season over season. Templates treat beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion categories rather than variations on apparel. And the collaboration model assumes the work crosses company boundaries, because in fashion it almost always does.

Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Both sets are vendor-published adoption signals rather than independent benchmarks. The difference is which industry they come from.

documents.t: Consider a contemporary label developing a 120-piece resort collection. The design team explores silhouettes and prints in the autumn; the production team needs catalog, lookbook, campaign, and social assets in the spring; a freelance photographer sets the visual direction; an agency handles paid social. FLORA is genuinely strong in the autumn half. Sketch-to-render, colorway exploration, and print and pattern replacement are exactly the design-stage problems a creative team has, and having 50+ models on one canvas makes exploration cheap. The spring half is where the shape of the product starts to matter. Batch across SKUs exists, but the casting depth is shallower, category templates outside apparel are thinner, and—most practically—every additional collaborator is a seat. With self-serve tiers capped at eight seats and per-seat prices running from $18 to $200 a month plus metered usage on top, adding the photographer, two agency people, and a merchandiser is a procurement decision rather than an invitation. Astria inverts the emphasis. It contributes little to the autumn exploration, and it is built for the spring: the approved treatment runs across the 120 pieces imported from Shopify or Google Drive, campaign and social extend the same direction, motion animates approved stills, and the photographer and agency work inside the brand workspace rather than against a seat count.

documents.t: This is FLORA's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Casting depth matters just as much: age range, body type, children's and extended-size casting are production requirements, not preferences, and a general on-model capability does not cover them.

Astria's brand workspaces are built for that cast of collaborators, with a multiplayer Board, named cursors, and live voice over the actual looks.

documents.t: FLORA's shape is a creative-suite subscription: per seat, per month, with metered usage credits layered on and enterprise beyond the eight-seat ceiling. documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Graswald

documents.t: Graswald describes itself as the AI production studio for fashion brands, and the workflow matches: a team establishes brand standards—custom avatars, lighting, studio scene, poses—then generates across the catalog, including batch runs driven by CSV upload. Supported output spans PDP on-model imagery, packshots, lookbooks, lifestyle content, and video, with 4K resolution and PIM/DAM integrations. The customer evidence is genuinely strong for this category. The VAUDE case study reports 50% lower content production costs and 30% more content published live, with the brand generating from flat-lays and factory sample photos on two custom avatars that replicate its studio scene digitally—work the internal team now runs in-house. The PUMA case study describes something more unusual: adapting central global creative to individual US retailer specifications for wholesale, so partners receive imagery that meets their guidelines without a round of rework. Two caveats a buyer should carry into a demo. The PUMA story, unlike the VAUDE one, publishes no quantitative outcomes. And the homepage headline figures—90% cost reduction, 10x faster, 100% brand consistency—are vendor absolutes. "100% brand consistency" is not a testable claim; your own difficult garments are.
documents.s: Graswald: enterprise brand standards, configured once

documents.t: Astria shares the configure-once thesis and diverges on who the system is for. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace that a creative director, an in-house team, an outside photographer, or an agency can all work in. The approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit, and it is designed to be handed over rather than maintained by one party. Coverage is the other divergence. Astria's templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work alongside apparel, so a brand with an accessories line or a beauty extension is not routing those categories elsewhere. Astria's Describe tool can turn a rights-cleared reference into usable creative direction while accounting for the products and models already loaded, which is a faster path from "match our last campaign" to a template than commissioning a new avatar build.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Graswald publishes named enterprise stories—VAUDE with real numbers, PUMA on wholesale localisation—plus a strategic partnership with Orendt Studios. That is a serious set of references for large-brand catalog work, and it is vendor-published rather than independently verified. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work on the platform. Also vendor-published. The distinction worth noting is the shape of the base: Graswald's evidence concentrates in large enterprises with internal content teams, Astria's spans brands and the external creatives they hire.

documents.t: Consider a mid-size brand whose visual direction comes from an outside photographer it has used for six seasons. The brand wants to produce most of its catalog and campaign imagery with AI, but it wants that photographer's eye encoded in the result, and it wants its own two-person ecommerce team running the work by spring. With Graswald, the path runs through the vendor: an enterprise conversation, then a collaboration to build custom avatars and replicate the studio scene and lighting digitally. That produces a strong result—VAUDE's story describes exactly this and the outcome was good—but the brand's photographer is not naturally a participant in it, and the configuration lives in an enterprise engagement rather than in a workspace the brand's creative partner can operate. With Astria, the photographer works directly in the brand's workspace: sets the casting, builds the templates, uses Describe to pull direction out of a rights-cleared reference from a previous season, and reviews with the ecommerce team on the multiplayer Board with live voice. When the season starts, the two-person team runs the approved treatment across the SKU set imported from Shopify or Google Drive. The photographer's judgment is now the brand's asset, and the handoff happened inside the tool rather than as a document.

documents.t: Lookgen's three-step flow is deliberately unglamorous: upload items in whatever form you have them—flat lay, hanger shot, ghost mannequin, straight off the rack—pick a virtual model, and generate. From there a stylist adjusts poses, swaps accessories, and fine-tunes, then extends the look to more camera angles and different sceneries before publishing. Two things distinguish it. First, the emphasis on complete outfits rather than single products: accessories can be added in one click, from the brand's own collection or generated, and the customer testimonials repeatedly describe showing shoppers styling options rather than individual garments. Lookgen says it was built in collaboration with professional stylists so that expertise sits inside the product, and the framing rings true. Second, the publishing path: Lookgen connects to a PIM and DAM to import, code, and publish automatically, which for a European multi-brand retailer is often the part that decides whether a tool gets used at all. Its published proof is a wall of named-person testimonials—WE Fashion, NAADAM, Esqualo, The English Hatter, Suitable, Arthur & Willemijn—which is a more checkable form of evidence than aggregate statistics, even though it remains vendor-published. Access is through a booked demo; no pricing is published.
documents.s: Lookgen: the look as the product

documents.t: Astria's unit of work is not the look but the treatment behind it. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved combination of casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, and format becomes the reusable thing. That is a superset of look-building in practice. Astria produces the styled on-model shots, and it also produces the campaign frames, editorial spreads, social crops, and motion from the same direction. Categories go beyond apparel plus accessories into beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, and luxury as full template disciplines, and the casting library spans ages and body types including children and extended sizes.

documents.t: Lookgen's testimonials name individuals at recognizable European retailers, which makes them unusually verifiable for vendor content—you can look those people up. Astria's public materials name fashion brands—Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, Nine West—alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published. documents.t: Consider a menswear retailer with 300 SKUs that merchandises by outfit: a jacket shown with the right shirt, trousers, and shoes, so shoppers buy three items instead of one. Lookgen is well aimed at this. A stylist builds the looks, swaps accessories, generates angle variants, and the results publish into the PIM without a manual handoff. For catalog merchandising of styled combinations, that is a tight, purpose-built loop, and the retailer's ecommerce team gets exactly the assets it needs. The gaps appear at the edges of the season. The spring campaign needs imagery with a point of view rather than a scenery swap. Social needs motion. The accessories line has a jewelry capsule that needs macro treatment, not one-click placement. A new hire needs to produce looks consistent with what the stylist established, and the direction lives in the stylist's choices rather than in a stored treatment. And the brand's freelance art director cannot join the work without a demo and a contract. With Astria, the styled looks come from an approved treatment that also produces the campaign, the editorial frames, the social crops, and the motion. Jewelry and beauty have their own template categories. The art director works inside the brand workspace, reviewing on the multiplayer Board with live voice, and what the stylist decided is stored rather than remembered.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Looklet

documents.t: Looklet has been doing this since 2009, and its architecture reflects that lineage. The workflow starts in a studio: garments are shot in a Looklet setup, with the company describing up to 100 items per day handled by one or two operators. Captured items are processed with automated quality control and a human check, with turnaround stated in hours. Only then does the styling step happen, in software where a team composes looks on digitized models—mixing garments shot at different times without reshooting—and exports with metadata for the storefront. The model library is the part competitors cannot easily replicate. Looklet's digitized models are real people captured with a large range of facial expressions and body movements, alongside a smaller set of AI-generated models. For a retailer with licensing sensitivities, digitized real models are a meaningfully different proposition from synthetic faces. The customer evidence is correspondingly serious. Looklet's Saks Fifth Avenue case study describes deployment across five studios, single-operator shoots replacing eight-person crews, and looks live within 6–24 hours. It is vendor-written, but the operational detail is specific enough to be checkable, and it describes exactly the buyer Looklet is built for.
documents.s: Looklet: digital styling on top of a capture operation

documents.t: Astria removes the capture step from the equation. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the inputs are the product photographs a brand already has. An approved look becomes a reusable treatment rather than a styling session repeated per item. The consequence is reach. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work rather than catalog PDPs alone, and brand references keep results anchored to the brand's visual language. The same approved treatment extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion, so the season's assets come from one direction instead of several disconnected production tracks.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Looklet's proof is enterprise retail: Saks Fifth Avenue, Holt Renfrew, and Stockmann, with outcomes framed around staffing, turnaround, and cost per look. That is credible evidence of industrial catalog production and it should be read as such. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them, including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Both sets are vendor-published adoption signals rather than independent benchmarks. They describe different jobs: Looklet's customers are running a photography operation more efficiently; Astria's are producing a brand's creative output.
documents.s: Public proof: retail operations versus brand production

documents.t: Consider a growing contemporary brand with roughly 500 SKUs a year. It needs catalog imagery, a seasonal lookbook, campaign assets, and social content, and it currently books a photographer twice a season. Choosing Looklet means choosing an operating model. Garments must reach a studio and be shot there; the enterprise tier bundles the hardware to make that possible in-house. Once that pipeline exists, catalog throughput is genuinely excellent and the per-look styling economics improve with volume. But the brand has taken on a capture operation—space, equipment, sample logistics, and operators—to solve what was, for it, a creative problem rather than a throughput problem. The lookbook, campaign, and social work still need a separate answer. Choosing Astria means the product photos the brand already produces become the input. Casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format get defined once and approved; the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive and runs against that treatment. The lookbook and campaign extend the same direction, motion animates stills that already passed review, and there is no sample-to-studio logistics chain in the middle.

Looklet's workflow assumes a capture step you operate; Astria's assumes product photography you already have. For a retail group amortizing five studios across tens of thousands of SKUs, Looklet's assumption is sound. For most brands, installing a capture operation to produce catalog imagery is a larger commitment than the problem warrants.

It is a throughput and licensing advantage, not a creative-direction verdict.

Astria treats all of those as expressions of one approved direction, which is why a brand can run the season from a single setup instead of routing each channel to a different supplier.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Lumoo

documents.t: Lumoo Air describes itself as a visual creation studio with a single clear promise: one prompt, studio-grade product photos, model shots, and video, generated, edited, and packaged for every channel. The workflow diagram on its homepage is the product in miniature—a source image fanning out into a side profile, a back view, a detail shot, a video, and social content, all connected in one pass. Around that sit sensible utilities: instant conversion between images, video, and try-ons, cropping and resizing to standard and custom ratios, colour adjustment for saturation, brightness, contrast, temperature and tint, and pre-built template packages for poses, video, transforms, and sizing. It also offers real-time collaboration on the same workflow, which is more than several larger competitors in this comparison provide. Pricing is published in euros and easy to read: 50 free credits with no card, then Lite at €15 a month for 100 credits, Basic at €70 for 500, Pro at €120 for 1,000, with custom plans from 2,000 to 5,000 credits starting at €220. The site converts those for you—Pro is roughly 600 images or 50 videos a month. One gap is worth naming. The homepage carries a "trusted by leading brands" banner, and in the material we reviewed no brands are named, and we found no case studies. That is common for an early product and it does mean a buyer has little to verify.
documents.s: Lumoo: one image, many outputs

documents.t: Astria's unit of work is not the image but the treatment. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved combination of casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, and format is what gets reused across a collection. Depth follows from that. The casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations and poses. Templates treat beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion categories. Campaign frames, social crops, and motion all extend the same direction, and review happens on a multiplayer Board with named cursors and live voice, with external photographers and agencies inside the same workspace.

documents.t: Lumoo's public evidence is currently thin: a trust banner without names and no case studies we could locate. This should not be read as a quality judgement—new products earn references over time—but it does leave a buyer with nothing to check. Astria's public materials name fashion brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published, and at least verifiable by looking.

documents.t: Consider a growing label with 150 styles going live in spring, needing four images per style, a handful of clips for social, and a small campaign set. Lumoo handles any single style beautifully. Upload the product photo, get the model shot, the back view, the detail crop, and a clip, adjust the colour, crop for each channel, done. For a founder producing a dozen assets a month this is a genuinely pleasant workflow with almost no learning curve. The arithmetic is where it turns. 150 styles at four images is 600 images—the entire Pro tier at €120 a month, before a single rejected frame, before the clips, before the campaign set. Custom plans exist and start at €220 for 2,000 credits, so the volume is servable; the question is whether a per-image meter is the right way to buy a season. And each of those 600 images is configured rather than derived: the template packages help with poses and sizing, but the brand's casting and styling decisions are re-entered rather than stored. With Astria, the treatment is approved once and the 150 styles run against it after importing from Shopify or Google Drive. The campaign set and social crops extend the same direction rather than being separate jobs, and the clips animate stills that already passed review.
